**Risk factors that the Mayo Clinic lists for *all three* aneurysm types (abdominal aortic, brain, and thoracic aortic) are:** | Risk factor | Evidence from Mayo Clinic | |-------------|---------------------------| | **Age** (older adults) | *Abdominal aortic aneurysm* – “Age. Abdominal aortic aneurysms occur most often in people age 65 and older.”
*Thoracic aortic aneurysm* – “Age. Thoracic aortic aneurysms occur most often in people age 65 and older.”
*Brain aneurysm* – “Age. Brain aneurysms can happen at any age. However, they’re more common in adults between ages 30 and 60.” | | **Smoking / tobacco use** | *Abdominal aortic aneurysm* – “Tobacco use. Smoking is the strongest risk factor for aortic aneurysms.”
*Thoracic aortic aneurysm* – “Smoking and tobacco use. If you smoke or chew tobacco … use tobacco also can worsen an aneurysm.”
*Brain aneurysm* – “Cigarette smoking. Smoking is a risk factor for brain aneurysms to form and for brain aneurysms to rupture.” | | **High blood pressure (hypertension)** | *Abdominal aortic aneurysm* – “High blood pressure. High blood pressure can damage and weaken the aorta’s walls.”
*Thoracic aortic aneurysm* – “High blood pressure. Increased blood pressure damages the blood vessels…raises the risk of an aneurysm.”
*Brain aneurysm* – “High blood pressure. This condition can weaken arteries. Aneurysms are more likely to form and to rupture in weakened arteries.” | | **Family history of aneurysm** | *Abdominal aortic aneurysm* – “Family history. Having a family history of abdominal aortic aneurysms increases the risk.”
*Thoracic aortic aneurysm* – “Family history. You’re more likely to get an aortic aneurysm…and rupture if you have a parent, brother, sister or child with one.”
*Brain aneurysm* – “Family history. The risk is higher if you have family members who have had a brain aneurysm.” | These four factors—older age, tobacco use, hypertension, and a family history of aneurysm—are explicitly mentioned as risk factors in all three Mayo Clinic disease pages. Other factors (e.g., genetic/connective‑tissue disorders, atherosclerosis, or being male/female) appear in one or two of the conditions but are **not** common to all three.
